title: "Reproducible Builds"

## Overview

Publishing an image is the biggest single step you can take towards
reproducibility. It largely solves the problem of getting your software to run on
other systems. Moreover, an image is a fixed snapshot, so anyone who pulls it
obtains an identical copy of the software and, in most cases, consistent runtime
behaviour.

For a publication, a single, well-annotated image may be sufficient. We
discuss how to record information about an image, in the form of *labels*,
below. In most cases, however, you will want images that can be *rebuilt*,
either to apply security patches to packages your application depends on, or to
release a new version with more features or bug fixes. Providing a rebuildable
image, i.e., a working `Containerfile`, also improves reusability, since it lets
others build on or adapt your image.

Care is needed when rebuilding, however, to prevent the software in an image
changing in an uncontrolled way. In this lesson we cover how to make
builds repeatable, so that containers provide a reproducible means for you to
both consume and share software. 

## Why builds change

The instructions of a `Containerfile` are evaluated at build time. This means
that the sources it draws on, such as the base image, packages or repositories,
can change between builds. For example:

- the base image referred to by a tag may be updated (rebuilt) by its owner
- a Python package installed with `pip` will default to the latest available
  version
- the files in a git repository that is downloaded may have been updated or
  replaced

As a consequence, the same `Containerfile` built weeks or months apart will, in
general, produce different images. In some cases, a source may disappear, resulting 
in later builds failing entirely.

The other side of the coin to the reliance on remote sources are the sources
which you control. In order for others to rebuild your image, all
material you use must be available to them, and your `Containerfile` publicly
accessible. This normally means including the `Containfile` in a repository alongside the source
code of your application. A repository containing *just* a `Containerfile` is
also fine if your build is a curated assembly of external sources and packages,
such as a particular Python environment used for a study in a paper.
Use only publicly accessible packages and source
URLs, and add any local files you `COPY` into the image to the same repository:
an image that depends on a file stored only on your own computer cannot be
rebuilt
by others.

## Pinning dependencies

*Pinning* means specifying an exact version of a dependency, rather than
using the default or latest version. It is recommended for the packages your
application directly relies on.

### Python packages

In `requirements.txt`, a package is pinned using `==` followed by a version
number. The script in `python-demo` from [Building Containers](building.qmd)
printed the installed NumPy version in the container logs. At the time of
writing this was `2.5.4`; if you ran the image you might go back
and check the container logs to compare the version installed in your case.

Assuming we were happy our application was
stable and tested with `2.5.4`, we would edit the requirements file to:

```bash
numpy==2.5.4
```

Each time the image is rebuilt, the same NumPy version is then used, so we can be
confident the Python script will behave in the same way. If we later wanted to
increase the NumPy version, for example to take advantage of a new feature,
it is advisable to publish the image with a new version tag (see below),
so that people using the software know that the image content has changed. 
You will have to practice pinning and tagging in the
[exercise](#exercise-republishing-python-demo) at the end of this lesson.

::: {.callout-tip collapse=true}
## Pinning indirect dependencies

Pinning dependencies does not pin their own dependencies. For complete
control, tools that produce *lock files* can be used, such as `pip-tools`
for Python packages. We do not cover them in this course.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Deterministic builds, not runs

The techniques in this lesson make the built image repeatable, not the output
of the software itself. The demo script in `python-demo` is non-deterministic,
so it gives different estimates of π on every run. Can you see how to fix this?
(The exercise below addresses this.)
:::

### System packages

Pinning system packages, i.e., packages installed for the base operating system, 
requires more care. Distributions such as Ubuntu and Debian do not keep outdated package
versions in their main repositories, and a pinned version that has been removed
will break your build.

Updates to system packages are primarily security patches, which you want, with only  small
risk of changing the behaviour of your application.
In most cases, then, it is simpler not to pin them.
This compromise is one reason it is important to test your image after
rebuilding, as discussed in the next module. 


### Downloaded software

Other software components can be fixed in a similar way. For example, the Fiji
ImageJ software provides a 'latest' download link of the form

```dockerfile
downloads.micron.ox.ac.uk/fiji_update/mirrors/fiji-latest/fiji-latest-linux64-jdk.zip
```

but also an archive of stable releases you can draw on:

```dockerfile
downloads.imagej.net/fiji/archive/stable/20250514-1821/fiji-stable-linux64-jdk.zip
```
Here, the date `2025-0514-1821` provides a fixed reference for the software
version.

### Base image

The base image can be fixed too. A GPU application, for example, can use a
specific NVIDIA image tag, such as `cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu24.04` that was
used in [Running Containers II](../01-introduction/running-containers-part-2.qmd#gpu-access-optional)),
the pin the version of the CUDA Toolkit.

In fact, the base image is typically the single largest dependency
of your application, so should be chosen carefully. Two general
recommendations are:

- Use a specific version tag, such as `python:3.13-slim`, rather than
  `latest`. Check the images registry page to ensure the tag you chose is
  sufficiently specific; `python:3.13` resolves to `python:3.13.x`, but
  for our demo at least we do not worry about the patch number varying.
- Prefer official or well-maintained images, from sources you can trust.
  On Docker Hub, look for *Official Image* or *Verified Publisher* badges.
  There is no official accreditation on GitHub's registry, but
  download counts and repository stars provide a proxy for popularity. Check that
  this popularity is consistent with what you would expect from that project.

![The `3.13-slim` tag of the [Python official container image](https://hub.docker.com/_/python/) is equivalent to the more specific `3.13.18-slim-trixie` tag](assets/python313-slim-tags.png)

Remember that even a specific version tag such as `python:3.13.18-slim-trixie`
may change over time, e.g., due to an update to the underlying operating system.
If you want to pin the base image precisely, you can use a *digest*, which is a
hash, prefixed by `sha256:`, identifying the exact content of an image. On GitHub, it is shown
on the details page of a package version, such as
that for [the `python-demo` image](https://github.com/piperfw/podman-desktop-course/pkgs/container/python-demo/1400793660?tag=latest).

A digest can be added to the `Containerfile` by appending it to the tag:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim@sha256:...
```

Similar to pinning system packages, the trade-off is that you will not
automatically receive fixes to the base image, and must manually
update the digest when needed. 
Hence, using a digest probably only necessary if you are preparing a reference for a
publication, or need a build to be exactly repeatable, for example to debug it.

## Curating tags and metadata

We now discuss how to tag and label your own images, so that each published
version can be identified.

### Descriptive tags to semantic versioning

Name-based tags like `:dev` or `:feature` are convenient while developing
locally, but use version tags when publishing. A common scheme [1] is
semantic versioning, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, starting from `0.0.1` for a development
realse or `1.0.0` for a first public stable release. Increase the patch
number for small fixes, the minor number for new features, and the major number
for significant changes that may break compatibility. In any case,
avoid relying on `:latest`
when pulling an image, since it points at different images over time.

::: {.callout-warning collapse=true}
## One software per image

Tags should be used to indicate different versions of an application. 
If you decide to package a different application in a container
you use, publish them as separate images.
:::

### Image metadata

*Metadata* provides auxiliary information about an image, and can be recorded
inside the image itself. This is achieved using the `LABEL` instruction in the
`Containerfile`, which defines a key-value pair to be included with the image.

The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines standard label names [2].
Here is a set for our demo image:

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="python-demo"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.description="Demo Python app to estimate pi"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="0.0.1"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.authors="Your Name"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/username/python-demo"
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
```

The `licenses` label takes an [SPDX licence identifier](https://spdx.org/licenses/),
such as `MIT`.

These should be placed near the end of the `Containerfile`, so that changing them does not
force the slow steps before them to run again. Registries and tools read these
labels. GitHub, for example, uses the description label as the package
description, and prompts you to add one if it is missing:

![Version 0.0.1 of `python-demo` with description, linked repository and MIT license](assets/github-description-and-license.png)

### Further considerations

Some labels record the *provenance* of an image, meaning where it came from and
how it was made: `source`, `version`, `revision` (the commit it was built from)
and `created` (the build time) [2].
These are easily left out of date when building and pushing manually. In the next module we look at 
filling `version` and `revision`  automatically as part of a
workflow. There we also cover other important aspects of releasing your software
openly, such as including a licence and citation information with your
repository.

## Balancing reproducibility and maintainability

Version pinning reveals there is a tension between reproducibility and maintainability. A fixed
environment is reproducible, but cannot receive security patches and
bug fixes. A reasonable approach is to pin selectively and upgrade deliberately: update on a schedule
or when new security patches or bug fixes become available,  test the result
and publish a new versioned image.

For research software in particular, it is becoming more common practice to mint
a versioned image when preparing a manuscript for publication.  That image is
the binary record of your 'software experiment', and the version you cite. The
software itself on the other hand can continue to be developed and updated.

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Reproducible outcomes, not identical inputs

An argument can be made that scientific reproducibility is about reproducible
outcomes, which does not require bitwise reproducibility of software. The laws
of Physics say that the motion of the planets is the same whether viewed from Paris or Rome,
not that the motion of the planets is the same provided one uses the same
telescope, lens manufacturer, etc.  An image lets anyone re-run your analysis
reliably, which is valuable. Your conclusions however should not depend on that
one environment. Useful science is robust.
:::

## Exercise: republishing `python-demo`

In this exercise you will make the `python-demo` image from [Building
Containers](building.qmd) more repeatable and identifiable, then republish it.

1. Run the current `python-demo` image twice, and compare the estimates of π in the
   logs. They will differ.
2. Pin NumPy in `requirements.txt` to the version shown in the logs.
3. Edit `script.py` so that the generator is seeded, e.g.,
   `rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)`.
4. Add `LABEL` instructions to your `Containerfile`, adapting the values above
   to your own name and repository. Omit `source` if you have no repository.
5. Rebuild the image, giving it the tag `0.0.1`, for example
   `ghcr.io/username/python-demo:0.0.1`.
6. Run the new image twice and compare the logs. The estimates should now be
   identical.
7. Push the new image, as in [Publishing Images](publishing.qmd).

**Check your work.** On your GitHub package page, you should see the new `0.0.1`
tag and the description from your label, with other labels included in the 
image manifest GitHub renders. You can compare your `0.0.1` package
to [this example](https://github.com/piperfw/podman-desktop-course/pkgs/container/python-demo/1400793660?tag=latest).
Note that `latest` still appears as a separate package version from the 
*earlier* image, which is one reason `latest` should not be relied on it.

<!--Note repeatable numbers with a fixed seed to `np.random` is only guaranteed for a particular NumPy version, which is why we pinned it first.-->
